claims.text: The coefficient of friction and wear rate of HEA coatings on transition-metal matrices vary non-monotonically with ambient temperature.
Initial tribological improvement with increasing temperature is caused by strain-rate softening and oxide formation.
Tribological performance degrades sharply after the onset of significant solid-solution softening and oxide-layer instability.
The proposed HEA coating is dense and nanocrystalline or equiatomic.
The proposed coating has high hardness and a stable solid-solution structure at room temperature.
Temperature-dependent wear is governed by competition between formation of a protective, self-healing tribo-oxide and thermally activated softening of the HEA matrix.
Thermal softening of the HEA matrix occurs through dislocation climb and cross-slip.
Between 25°C and 400°C, frictional heating promotes rapid formation of a continuous, adherent oxide tribofilm.
The oxide tribofilm reduces direct metal-to-metal contact and acts as a solid lubricant.
Above a critical temperature, reduced Peierls stress and activation of multiple slip systems cause significant thermal softening.
Above the critical temperature, coating yield strength decreases faster than the oxide layer can reform or remain adherent.
Loss of matrix strength causes tribofilm breakdown, increased adhesive wear, and plastic deformation of the substrate.
The coefficient of friction decreases as temperature rises toward approximately 400°C and then increases sharply above the critical temperature.
The specific wear rate reaches a minimum at approximately 400°C and increases exponentially above the critical temperature.
The degradation regime corresponds to a transition from oxidative wear to severe adhesive and abrasive wear.
At room temperature, wear is dominated by mild abrasive and adhesive mechanisms without significant thermal oxide formation.
The degradation boundary occurs when coating yield strength falls below the critical shear stress needed to maintain tribo-oxide integrity.
For most Cr- or Al-containing HEAs in air, the critical degradation temperature is typically between 500°C and 600°C.
Refractory additions such as W or Mo may increase the critical degradation temperature.
Sliding velocity affects the critical temperature by changing asperity flash temperature relative to bulk ambient temperature.
